item.question: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 5 o'clock?
steps: A full turn of the clock face is 360 degrees and it has 12 hours, so one hour is 360 ÷ 12 = 30 degrees.
At 5 o'clock the hands are 5 hours apart, so the angle is 5 × 30 = 150 degrees.
item.text:
Worked example: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 5 o'clock?
1. A full turn of the clock face is 360 degrees and it has 12 hours, so one hour is 360 ÷ 12 = 30 degrees.
2. At 5 o'clock the hands are 5 hours apart, so the angle is 5 × 30 = 150 degrees.
Answer: 150 degrees

And at 4 o'clock? 6 o'clock? c. Explore other angles made by the hands of a clock. a) At 1 o'clock the angle between the hands is 30°. steps_tex: A clock face is one full turn of $360^\circ$, cut by the $12$ numbers into $12$ equal gaps.
One gap is $360 \div 12 = 30$ degrees. At $1\text{ o'clock}$ the hands are $1$ gap apart, so the angle is $1 \times 30^\circ = 30^\circ$.
At $2\text{ o'clock}$ the hands are $2$ gaps apart: $2 \times 30^\circ = 60^\circ$.
At $4\text{ o'clock}$ the hands are $4$ gaps apart: $4 \times 30^\circ = 120^\circ$.
At $6\text{ o'clock}$ the hands are $6$ gaps apart: $6 \times 30^\circ = 180^\circ$.
Other hours work the same way: at $3\text{ o'clock}$, $3 \times 30^\circ = 90^\circ$.
At $9\text{ o'clock}$, $9 \times 30^\circ = 270^\circ$ one way round, and the other way round is $360^\circ - 270^\circ = 90^\circ$.
item.answer_tex: $(a)$: The clock's $360^\circ$ is divided into $12$ equal parts, so the angle between two successive numbers is $\frac{360}{12} = 30^\circ$. $(b)$: $2\text{ o'clock} = 60^\circ$, $4\text{ o'clock} = 120^\circ$, $6\text{ o'clock} = 180^\circ$. $(c)$: e.g. $3\text{ o'clock} = 90^\circ$, $9\text{ o'clock} = 270^\circ$.
steps: A clock face is one full turn of 360°, cut by the 12 numbers into 12 equal gaps.
One gap is 360 ÷ 12 = 30 degrees. At 1 o'clock the hands are 1 gap apart, so the angle is 1 × 30° = 30°.
At 2 o'clock the hands are 2 gaps apart: 2 × 30° = 60°.
At 4 o'clock the hands are 4 gaps apart: 4 × 30° = 120°.
At 6 o'clock the hands are 6 gaps apart: 6 × 30° = 180°.
Other hours work the same way: at 3 o'clock, 3 × 30° = 90°.
At 9 o'clock, 9 × 30° = 270° one way round, and the other way round is 360° − 270° = 90°.
item.answer: a. The clock's 360° is divided into 12 equal parts, so the angle between two successive numbers is 360/12 = 30°. b. 2 o'clock = 60°, 4 o'clock = 120°, 6 o'clock = 180°. c. e.g. 3 o'clock = 90°, 9 o'clock = 270°.
item.text:
$1$. A clock face is one full turn of $360^\circ$, cut by the $12$ numbers into $12$ equal gaps.
$2$. One gap is $360 \div 12 = 30$ degrees. At $1\text{ o'clock}$ the hands are $1$ gap apart, so the angle is $1 \times 30^\circ = 30^\circ$.
$3$. At $2\text{ o'clock}$ the hands are $2$ gaps apart: $2 \times 30^\circ = 60^\circ$.
$4$. At $4\text{ o'clock}$ the hands are $4$ gaps apart: $4 \times 30^\circ = 120^\circ$.
$5$. At $6\text{ o'clock}$ the hands are $6$ gaps apart: $6 \times 30^\circ = 180^\circ$.
$6$. Other hours work the same way: at $3\text{ o'clock}$, $3 \times 30^\circ = 90^\circ$.
$7$. At $9\text{ o'clock}$, $9 \times 30^\circ = 270^\circ$ one way round, and the other way round is $360^\circ - 270^\circ = 90^\circ$.
Answer: $(a)$: The clock's $360^\circ$ is divided into $12$ equal parts, so the angle between two successive numbers is $\frac{360}{12} = 30^\circ$. $(b)$: $2\text{ o'clock} = 60^\circ$, $4\text{ o'clock} = 120^\circ$, $6\text{ o'clock} = 180^\circ$. $(c)$: e.g. $3\text{ o'clock} = 90^\circ$, $9\text{ o'clock} = 270^\circ$.

steps_tex: The door turns about the place where it meets the wall, the hinge, and this place does not move.
The two lines that make the opening are the edge of the door and the wall, so they are the two arms.
Open the door wider: the opening between its edge and the wall grows, so the amount a door is open is an angle.
Check with the closed door: its edge lies along the wall, so there is no opening.

item.question: Observe the images below where there is an insect and its rotated version. Can angles be used to describe the amount of rotation? How? What will be the arms of the angle and the vertex? Hint: Observe the horizontal line touching the insects.
steps_tex: Sample answer: the horizontal line touching the insects is one arm of the angle.
Draw a line along the rotated insect; this line is the other arm.
The two arms meet at the point that does not move when the insect turns; this point of rotation on the line is the vertex, and the arc between the arms shows the amount of rotation.
Check by turning the insect back: the arc shrinks to nothing, because the two arms lie on each other.
item.answer_tex: Yes. Open-ended. E.g. the horizontal line is one arm and the line along the rotated insect is the other arm, with the vertex at the point of rotation on the line.

item.question: Angle guessing game with two teams. Team 1 secretly chooses an angle measure, for example 49°, and makes an angle with that measure using a protractor without Team 2 being able to see it. Team 2 now gets to look at the angle. They have to quickly discuss and guess the number of degrees in the angle (without using a protractor!). Team 1 now demonstrates the true measure of the angle with a protractor. Team 2 scores the number of points that is the absolute difference in degrees between their guess and the correct measure. For example, if Team 2 guesses 39°, then they score 10 points (49°−39°). Each team gets five turns. The winner is the team with the lowest score.
steps: Team 1 makes a secret angle
Team 2 guesses
Score = absolute difference between guess and true measure
Five turns each; lowest score wins
